blocks.text: The cardiac jelly is an acellular matrix that is secreted by the myocardium in the developing heart.
**Cardiac Jelly (CJ):** A gelatinous, cell-free extracellular matrix filling the myoendocardial space of the embryonic heart tube.
**Function:**

items.text: Acts as a hydraulic skeleton, providing structural support during early heart development. (Option A)
Facilitates end-systolic occlusion of the embryonic heart lumen, improving pumping efficiency. (Option B)
Stores elastic energy during systole, aiding the refilling phase of the heart. (Option C)

blocks.text: Septum primum (Label A) grows first and contributes to the division of the atria. The septum secundum (Label B) grows later and overlaps the septum primum, forming the foramen ovale, which allows right-to-left blood flow in fetal life.
Septum Primum

Formed as a sickle-shaped fold from the roof and dorsal wall of the primitive atrium due to pressure from the bulbus cordis. Grows downward toward the atrioventricular (AV) canal and septum intermedium, fusing with the latter.
Ostium Primum
Before the septum primum reaches and fuses with the septum intermedium, a gap (foramen primum) allows blood flow between the right and left atria.
Ostium Secundum
Upper part of the septum primum breaks down, creating a new gap (foramen secundum) before the foramen primum closes. The septum primum now has a free upper edge.
Septum Secundum
Grows down from the roof of the atrial chamber, to the right of the septum primum, overlapping the free upper edge of the septum primum as it grows.
Foramen Ovale Formation
Overlapping septa create the foramen ovale, allowing blood to flow from right to left atrium during fetal life, preventing left-to-right flow. Patent throughout fetal life.
Obliteration of Foramen Ovale

Post-birth, the left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs, increasing pressure in this chamber greater than the right atrium, causing fusion of the septum primum and septum secundum, closing the foramen ovale. Annulus ovalis (adults) corresponds to the lower free edge of the septum secundum, while the fossa ovalis represents the septum primum.
Ostium secundum defect is the most common significant ASD characterized by a large atrial opening.
Defects in Interatrial Septal Development

Atrial Septal Defect (ASD): Varies from total absence of the atrial septum to small openings, such as probe patency of the oval foramen. Most significant defect: Ostium secundum defect, characterized by a large opening between the left and right atria.
Causes:

items.text: Excessive cell death and resorption of the septum primum.
Inadequate development of the septum secundum.

blocks.text: Complete Absence of Atrial Septum
Known as common atrium or cor triloculare biventriculare. Result from complete failure of the septum primum and septum secundum to form.
Premature Closure of Foramen Ovale
It can occur during prenatal life. Results in:

items.text: Massive hypertrophy of the right atrium and ventricle.
Underdevelopment of the left side of the heart.
Often leads to death shortly after birth.

blocks.text: **Ostium primum defect (Option A):** Accounts for about 10% of septal defects and develops due to a deficiency in tissue near the atrioventricular valves, making it less common than ostium secundum.

**Sinus venosus defect (Option B):** is located outside the fossa ovalis on the right septal surface. It is associated with anomalous right upper pulmonary venous return rather than a large atrial opening between the atria.

**Coronary Sinus Defect (Option C):** is located in the wall separating the coronary sinus from the left atrium; it may be fenestrated or absent and does not create a significant opening between the left and right atria.
Limbus fossa ovalis is the raised ridge surrounding the fossa ovalis.

**Fossa Ovalis:** (Option C) Depressed area located in the lower portion of the right atrial side of the interatrial septum. Remnant of the foramen ovale. Septum primum which is on the left atrial side, forms the floor of the fossa ovalis.
**Limbus Fossa Ovalis:** (Option D) A raised ridge (annulus) that surrounds the perimeter of the fossa ovalis. It is formed from the septum secundum, an infolding of the atrial roof.
**Septum primum (Option A):** forms the floor of the fossa ovalis, not the raised ridge surrounding it.
**Septum secundum (Option B):** contributes to the formation of the limbus fossa ovalis but does not directly appear as a raised ridge itself.

The spiraling of the aorticopulmonary septum positions the pulmonary trunk anteriorly and to the left of the aorta. This arrangement is crucial for separating the pulmonary and systemic circulations. The bulbus cordis elongates into three segments:

items.text: Proximal part forms bulboventricular chamber
Middle part: Conus cordis (outflow tract)
Distal part (Truncus arteriosus) develops into the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk

blocks.text: Truncus arteriosus undergoes septation and spiraling. There are two swellings along the truncus arteriosus- truncal swellings distally and conal swellings proximally.

The truncal swellings, resembling endocardial cushions, divide the lumen into the proximal ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk. The fusion of truncal and conal swellings establishes the pulmonary trunk’s origin from the right ventricle and the aorta’s origin from the left ventricle, with aortopulmonary valves forming at these fusion lines.
Spiraling of the septum allows the pulmonary trunk to cross anterior and to the left of the aorta. (Option C)
Failure of neural crest cells to migrate or disruptions to the aorticopulmonary septum leads to congenital heart disease
Septation defects:

items.text: **Persistent truncus arteriosus:** Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to form
**Tetralogy of Fallot:** Anterior and cephalad deviation of the aorticopulmonary septum. Comprises four defects linked to abnormalities:
VSD
Overriding aorta
Pulmonary stenosis
Right ventricular hypertrophy
**Double outlet right ventricle**

blocks.text: Spiraling defects:
**Transposition of the great vessels:** Positions of the aorta and pulmonary artery are switched due to errors in truncus arteriosus division.
**The pulmonary trunk moves posteriorly (Option A):** The pulmonary trunk moves anteriorly.

**The aorta moves to the right side of the body (Option B):** The aorta does end up in a more rightward position relative to the pulmonary trunk, but it does not specifically move to the right side of the body.
**There is no change in the position of either vessel (Option D):** The spiraling process specifically reorganizes the positions of the pulmonary trunk and aorta.

In this scenario, the newborn exhibits significant cyanosis and a single large vessel which is suggestive of persistent truncus arteriosus. It resulted from the failure of the conotruncal ridges to develop, which prevents the proper division of the outflow tracts into the aorta and pulmonary artery, leading to the mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
Aorticopulmonary septum anomalies
1) Tetralogy of Fallot
Most common conotruncal heart defect. Cause: Due to unequal division of the conus and anterior displacement of the septum. (Option D) Features four cardiovascular issues:

items.text: Pulmonary infundibular stenosis
Overriding aorta
Ventricular septal defect (VSD)
Right ventricular hypertrophy

blocks.text: Tetralogy along with ASD is known as pentalogy of fallot. Common in individuals with Alagille syndrome (also features liver abnormalities and distinctive facial traits). Often associated with a JAG1 gene mutation affecting neural crest cells.
2) Persistent Truncus Arteriosus

Cause: Failure of conotruncal ridges to form. (Option B) Features: Leads to a single outflow tract and a defective interventricular septum. The truncus overrides both ventricles. Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood combine, with lung-bound blood entering systemic circulation. Results in congenital cyanotic heart disease.
3) Transposition of the Great Vessels

Cause: Occurs when the conotruncal septum fails to spiral correctly. (Option C) Features:s Aorta connects to the right ventricle, pulmonary artery connects to the left ventricle. Patients cannot survive because deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium through the superior and inferior vena cavae, then flows to the right ventricle and into the ascending aorta, bypassing the lungs completely. PDA is essential for survival, allowing blood flow to the lungs for oxygenation.
**Failure of the atrioventricular septum to form (Option A):** refers to atrioventricular septal defects, which involve issues in the separation of the atria and ventricles, not the outflow tracts.
The posterior part of the membranous septum separates the left ventricle from the right atrium, not the right ventricle from the left atrium.
Formation of Interventricular Septum
The interventricular septum consists of three parts:

items.text: Muscular part
Bulbar part
Membranous part

blocks.text: 1. Muscular Part

Septum grows upward from the floor of the bulboventricular cavity, dividing it into right and left halves. (Option A) This growth is driven by passive dilation and hemodynamic forces. Septum fuses with the atrioventricular (AV) cushions (septum intermedium).
Interventricular foramen forms between the two ventricles at the upper margin of the septum and is eventually closed by the septum intermedium and proximal bulbar septum. (Option D)
2. Bulbar Part

Two bulbar ridges (right and left) arise from the wall of the bulboventricular cavity. These ridges fuse to form the proximal bulbar septum, which grows downward toward the muscular septum but leaves a gap. (Option B)
3. Membranous Part
The gap between the muscular septum and the bulbar septum is filled by tissue from the AV cushions and bulbar ridges. Membranous septum consists of:

items.text: Anterior part: Separates the right and left ventricles.
Posterior part: Separates the left ventricle from the right atrium. (Option C)

blocks.text: Mechanism of Septal Formation
Interventricular septum is likely formed by the downward enlargement of the right and left ventricular cavities on either side of the septum, rather than by active septal growth itself.

Ductus arteriosus allows most blood from the right ventricle to bypass the lungs by shunting it directly into the aorta, ensuring efficient delivery of oxygenated blood to the fetal brain and upper body.
Fetal Circulation:

items.text: **Oxygenated Blood Flow:** Placenta → Umbilical Vein → Ductus Venosus (bypasses liver) → Inferior Vena Cava → Right Atrium → Foramen Ovale → Left Atrium → Left Ventricle → Ascending Aorta → Oxygen to head, neck, and upper limbs

**Deoxygenated Blood Flow:** Superior Vena Cava (SVC) → Right Atrium → Right Ventricle → Pulmonary Trunk → Ductus Arteriosus (bypass pulmonary circulation) → Descending Aorta → Lower body → Umbilical Arteries → Placenta (for oxygenation)

blocks.text: Peculiarities of Fetal Circulation

items.text: **Ductus Venosus:** Directs blood to the inferior vena cava, bypassing the liver and preserving oxygen content. (Option A)
**Foramen Ovale:** Allows equal distribution of blood to both sides of the heart, ensuring more oxygenated blood reaches vital organs in the upper body. (Option C)
**Ductus Arteriosus:** Directs blood from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, bypassing the lungs and allowing blood to flow to the placenta for oxygenation. (Option B)

blocks.text: More oxygenated blood flows to the upper limbs, resulting in longer upper limbs compared to lower limbs in the fetus.

**Umbilical vein (Option D):** carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus, but it doesn’t play a role in shunting blood past the lungs. Its function is to deliver oxygenated blood to the fetal circulation through the ductus venosus.

A machinery-like murmur in a neonate along with cyanosis and rapid breathing suggests patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). PDA is a fetal vessel connecting the pulmonary artery to the aorta that normally closes soon after birth. If it remains open (patent), it causes a left-to-right shunt (oxygenated blood from the aorta flows back into the pulmonary artery), leading to volume overload in the lungs, causing cyanosis and respiratory distress.

Persistent foramen ovale typically causes a different murmur and shunting pattern; closure of ductus venosus affects liver blood flow; malrotation of great arteries affects vessel positioning, not shunting or murmur.
Changes in the Circulation at Birth
Umbilical Arteries
Thick muscle walls of the umbilical arteries contract immediately after birth, occluding their lumen. This prevents the loss of fetal blood into the placenta.
Umbilical Vein and Ductus Venosus
Lumen of the umbilical vein and ductus venosus occludes a few minutes after birth, allowing time for fetal blood from the placenta to return to the fetus.
Ductus Arteriosus

Closes initially due to muscle contraction in the vessel wall, and later, intimal proliferation permanently obliterates the lumen, redirecting blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for oxygenation.
Pulmonary Vessels
Increase in size, allowing more blood to reach the left atrium from the lungs, increasing left atrial pressure.
Foramen Ovale

Increased pressure in the left atrium (due to lung circulation) and reduced pressure in the right atrium (due to cessation of placental blood flow) lead to the closure of the valve of the foramen ovale.
Fetal Circulatory Shunts and Their Changes After Birth

rows: Shunts blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta, bypassing pulmonary circulation.
Shunts blood from the right atrium to the left atrium
Shunts blood from the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava, bypassing the liver
Carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus
Carries deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta

Proximal part: Superior vesical artery
Distal part: Medial umbilical ligaments

blocks.text: Persistent foramen ovale (Option A) allows the shunting of blood from the right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the lungs. While it can cause cyanosis, the clinical presentation usually doesn't include a machinery murmur, and it is typically asymptomatic or mild compared to PDA.
Closure of ductus venosus (Option C) occurs normally after birth and redirects blood flow, but it does not cause shunting or significant symptoms like cyanosis or a murmur.

**Malrotation of the great arteries (Option D):** is a form of congenital heart defect that can cause cyanosis, but it would typically be detected earlier, often with profound cyanosis from birth. Unlike PDA, it does not present with a machinery-like murmur and does not involve a left-to-right shunt.
Cervical Pleura
Extends from the inner border of the 1st rib. Covers the apex of the lung. Passes downwards and medially to continue with the mediastinal pleura.
Pleural Cupola
Forms a cup-like dome over the apex of the lung. The summit of the dome reaches 2 to 3 cm higher than the medial third of the clavicle, at the level of the neck of the first rib.
Suprapleural Membrane (Sibson’s Fascia)

Covers the cervical pleura externally. A musculo-fascial expansion derived from the scalenus minimus muscle and endothoracic fascia. Extends from the tip of the transverse process of the 7th cervical vertebra to the inner border of the 1st rib. Medially continuous with the pretracheal fascia by the side of the trachea.
Relation to Structures
All structures related to the apex of the lung are superficial to the suprapleural membrane.
Pleura Structure and Function
Visceral Pleura
Surrounds lung tissue. Composed of a single mesothelial cell layer. Blood supply from bronchial arteries.
Parietal Pleura
Lines the inner chest wall. Contains stomata that drain pleural fluid into lymphatic capillaries. Connective tissue present; innervated by sensory nerve fibers.
Pleural Fluid

items.text: **Normal Volume:** 0.1 to 0.2 mL/kg.
**Inflow Rate:** 0.5 mL/hr in adults.
**Maximal Removal Rate:** 0.28 mL/kg/hr.

blocks.text: Accumulates when inflow exceeds removal (due to increased plasma filtration or impaired lymphatic drainage).
Lymphatic Drainage

Lymph drains into regional lymph nodes along the sternum or vertebra, then into the thoracic and right lymphatic ducts. Lymphatic vessels are 10-12 µm in diameter, large enough for intact erythrocytes.
Innervation
Visceral Pleura
No connective tissue; innervated by the vagus nerve, insensitive to pain.
Parietal Pleura
Connective tissue; innervated by intercostal nerves and phrenic nerve.
**Phrenic Nerve:** Predominantly innervates the central diaphragmatic region, referred pain to the ipsilateral shoulder.
Pleural Membrane Function
Allows frictionless movement of the lungs relative to the chest wall during respiration.
**Inspiration:** Negative pressure in the pleural space leads to lung expansion, allowing air to enter the lungs
Cardiac ganglion of Wrisberg, also called the juxta ductal body or the aortico-pulmonary ganglionic mass.
Cardiac Plexuses
Superficial Cardiac Plexus
**Location:** Below the arch of the aorta, in front of the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk, to the right of the ligamentum arteriosum (Option A)
**Cardiac Ganglion of Wrisberg:** Located close to the ligamentum arteriosum.
**Formation:**

items.text: (a) Superior cervical cardiac branch of the left cervical sympathetic trunk.
(b) Inferior cervical cardiac branch of the left vagus nerve.

blocks.text: **Distribution:** (Option C) (a) Deep cardiac plexus. (b) Right coronary artery. (c) Left anterior pulmonary plexus.
Deep Cardiac Plexus
**Location:** In front of the bifurcation of the trachea, behind the arch of the aorta.
**Formation:**

items.text: (a) Cardiac branches from three cervical and upper 4-5 thoracic ganglia of the sympathetic chains (except the superior cervical cardiac branch of the left sympathetic chain) (Option D)
(b) Cardiac branches from the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerves (except the inferior cervical cardiac branch of the left vagus nerve) (Option B)

blocks.text: **Distribution:** Right and left halves of the plexus: (a) Corresponding coronary arteries. (b) Pulmonary plexus. (c) Separate branches to the atria.

At this level, the aortic arch is usually seen, and the trachea begins to bifurcate into the right and left main bronchi.
Level of the Thoracic Inlet
This is at the top of the thoracic cavity, where the trachea and esophagus enter.
Level of the Aortic Arch
Located around the T4-T5 vertebral level, where the aorta arches over the left main bronchus.
Level of the Carina
At the T5-T6 level, this is where the trachea bifurcates into the right and left main bronchi.
Level of the Heart
The heart is typically seen from T6 to T9. You can identify the chambers (right atrium, left atrium, ventricles) and major vessels (aorta, pulmonary arteries).
Level of the Diaphragm
The diaphragm typically corresponds to the T10 vertebral level, which can help in distinguishing between thoracic and abdominal structures.
Level of the Esophagus
The esophagus runs along the midline and can be seen at various levels, usually starting from the cervical region down to T10.
Level of the Thoracic Spine
The thoracic vertebrae can be used as references; typically, there are 12 thoracic vertebrae.
**T1-T2 (Option A):** This level generally shows the upper mediastinum, including parts of the great vessels, but the aortic arch is not typically prominent.
**T5-T6 (Option C):** Here, the main bronchi are visible, but the aortic arch may not be well-defined.
**T7-T8 (Option D):** This level typically shows the lower mediastinum and may not include the aortic arch or the bifurcation of the trachea.

The left lung shows an impression from the aortic arch, which arches over the left main bronchus. Lung impressions refer to the indentations or impressions made on the surface of the lungs by adjacent structures in the thoracic cavity.

rows: Cardiac Impression (Left Ventricle, Auricle, part of Right Ventricle)

blocks.text: The presence of distended chest wall veins (collaterals) is highly indicative of increased venous pressure, commonly associated with superior vena cava (SVC) obstruction. In this case, the history of a mediastinal mass and metastasis suggests that the mass is compressing the SVC, leading to venous obstruction.
This obstruction can cause the characteristic collateral circulation (distended chest wall veins) to develop, as the body attempts to reroute blood flow to bypass the obstruction.
The illustration below shows signs of SVC obstruction

**Right heart failure (Option A):** While this can cause jugular distension, it typically does not lead to the development of prominent chest wall collaterals without other signs of systemic congestion.
**Pulmonary embolism (Option C):** This may cause acute respiratory distress but does not typically lead to distended chest wall veins or collaterals.

**Thoracic aortic aneurysm (Option D):** This may cause symptoms related to compression of surrounding structures but does not specifically account for the venous distension seen with SVC obstruction.

If the pleural effusion fluid is chylous (chyle), it indicates leakage of lymphatic fluid, often due to disruption or injury to the thoracic duct. Chylothorax is a condition where chyle accumulates in the pleural space, leading to pleural effusion. The thoracic duct drains lymph into the junction of the left subclavian vein and left internal jugular vein.
Thoracic duct

The thoracic duct starts as the cisterna chyli in the abdomen at the lower border of the T12 vertebra. It ascends through the aortic opening of the diaphragm. It initially runs on the right side of the descending aorta in the posterior mediastinum. At the T4 vertebra, it crosses from the right to the left side behind the esophagus. It continues upward along the left border of the esophagus to the root of the neck.

At the root of the neck, it arches laterally at the C7 vertebra, in front of the vertebral arteries and behind the carotid system. The duct collects lymph from the left jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks. It descends in front of the first part of the left subclavian artery.
It ends by draining into the junction of the left subclavian vein and the left internal jugular vein. (Option A, C, & D ruled out)
The thoracic duct carries lymph from the lower limbs, pelvic cavity, abdominal cavity, and the left side of the thorax, head, neck, and arm.
The right lymphatic duct does not drain the right abdomen; this region is typically drained by the thoracic duct, which handles lymph from the lower half of the body, including the abdomen.
Right Lymphatic Duct

The right lymphatic duct may form from the convergence of the right jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks. These trunks drain lymph from the right side of the head and neck, the right upper limb, and the right side of the thorax. When present, the right lymphatic duct is approximately 0.5 inches (1.3 cm) long. It opens into the beginning of the right brachiocephalic vein.
Alternatively, the lymphatic trunks may drain directly into the major veins at the root of the neck.
The superior hemiazygos vein drains into the azygos vein at the level of the seventh thoracic vertebra.
Azygos Vein

The origin of the azygos vein can vary, often starting from the union of the right ascending lumbar vein and the right subcostal vein in the abdomen. It ascends through the aortic opening in the diaphragm, on the right side of the aorta. The vein continues to rise until it reaches the level of the fifth thoracic vertebra. At this level, the azygos vein arches forward above the root of the right lung. It drains into the posterior surface of the superior vena cava. (Option A ruled out)
**Tributaries:**

items.text: The eight lower right intercostal veins
The right superior intercostal vein
The superior and inferior hemiazygos veins
Mediastinal veins.
Pericardial veins
Right subcostal vein.
Right bronchial vein.
Right ascending lumbar vein.

blocks.text: If there is an obstruction of the SVC, the azygos vein acts as the primary collateral pathway to redirect blood from the upper half of the body to the IVC. (Option D ruled out)
Inferior Hemiazygos Vein

The inferior hemiazygos vein is formed by the union of the left ascending lumbar vein and the left subcostal vein in the abdomen. It ascends through the left crus of the diaphragm and, around the level of the eighth thoracic vertebra, it turns to the right to join the azygos vein, receiving tributaries from the lower left intercostal and mediastinal veins. (Option B ruled out)
Superior Hemiazygos Vein

The superior hemiazygos vein is created by the union of the left superior intercostal vein and the fourth to eighth intercostal veins. It drains into the azygos vein at the level of the seventh thoracic vertebra.
Afferent fibers transmit sensory information from both the upper and lower surfaces of the diaphragm, as well as from the pericardium and mediastinal pleura and not from the liver capsule.
Phrenic Nerve
The phrenic nerves contain both efferent (motor) and afferent (sensory) fibers. (Option A ruled out) The efferent fibers provide the sole motor supply to the diaphragm muscle. (Option B ruled out)

The afferent fibers transmit sensory information to the central nervous system from the peritoneum covering the diaphragm's undersurface, the pleura on the diaphragm's upper surface, and the pericardium and mediastinal parietal pleura.
Paralysis of the phrenic nerve may result from pressure from malignant tumors in the mediastinum. (Option D ruled out)

Historically, surgical methods like crushing or sectioning the nerve in the neck were used to treat lung tuberculosis affecting the lower lobes, leading to diaphragm paralysis on that side. This causes the elevated, immobile dome of the diaphragm to provide rest to the affected lung.
